common_name: Double-Flowered Chameleon Plant (Flore Pleno Fish Mint)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into consistently moist to boggy soil in partial to full shade, ideally inside a buried barrier or sunken container; this plain-green, double-flowered selection spreads by rhizome just as readily as the species and the variegated 'Chameleon'.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, confining the rhizomes with a buried barrier or large sunken container. Unlike the familiar red-and-cream 'Chameleon' sport, 'Flore Pleno' keeps plain heart-shaped green leaves but produces unusually showy flower heads, each tiny true flower spike surrounded by multiple layers of white petal-like bracts that give a fuller, more camellia-like bloom than the single-bracted wild form. It carries the same tangy, citrus-coriander aroma in its foliage and can be harvested the same way for Vietnamese and Chinese dishes, though it is grown chiefly for the extended, more decorative bract display through summer. Keep soil constantly wet at a pond margin or rain garden and divide every year or two to prevent the planting from thinning in the center.

planting.note: Divide rooted suckers in spring or plant container-grown stock into moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to filtered sun after frost danger passes; the cream-margined leaves scorch in hot, direct afternoon sun and the variegation is noticeably less cold-hardy than the plain-green species, so site it with some wind and sun protection.

directions: Plant rooted suckers or container-grown stock in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun in spring, sheltering the planting from strong wind and the hottest afternoon sun. 'Variegata' carries the same enormous, deeply lobed, felt-backed tropical leaves as the species but with irregular creamy-white margins and flecking that make it a striking specimen for a shaded courtyard or jungle-style border. It is noticeably less vigorous and less cold-hardy than plain rice paper plant or the giant-leaved 'Steroidal Giant' selection, so give it a bit more winter protection and avoid exposing young variegated growth to late frost. Remove any shoots that revert to solid green promptly, since reverted growth is more vigorous and will eventually crowd out the variegated stems.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring into cool, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath high canopy; this Japanese woodland relative of Rhododendron resents hot sun, alkaline soil, and summer drought.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring into cool, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath the high canopy of a woodland garden, matching its native habitat in the mountain forests of Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu. Menziesia ciliicalyx is a deciduous Ericaceae shrub with soft-haired, finely toothed leaves and nodding clusters of small, urn-shaped flowers in late spring that range from pale yellow-green to dusky purple-pink depending on the form, followed by orange-red fall foliage color. It pairs naturally with Japanese maples, enkianthus, and dwarf rhododendrons in an acidic woodland or rock-garden setting, and needs only an annual top-dressing of leaf mold or pine duff rather than fertilizer. Avoid wet feet in winter and any lime-containing soil amendment, both of which quickly stress this otherwise trouble-free, slow-growing shrub.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs just below the soil surface in gritty, very well-drained alpine mix in full sun to light shade in fall; this diminutive Drakensberg-region species wants a cool, bright winter growing season followed by a dry summer dormancy and is best grown in a pot, raised bed, or alpine house in climates with wet summers.

directions: Plant small bulbs just below the surface of a gritty, fast-draining alpine or cactus mix in full sun to light shade in fall, allowing the foliage to grow through the cool winter months. Albuca humilis is a true miniature among the albucas, native to high, cold grasslands of the Drakensberg and Lesotho highlands, forming a tuft of a few narrow, slightly fleshy leaves and sending up a short stem of a few nodding, bell-shaped white flowers with a central green stripe on each petal in spring. Its high-altitude origin gives it more cold tolerance than most winter-growing Cape albucas, but it still needs a bone-dry summer rest once the leaves yellow and die back. Grow it in a shallow pan among other small rock-garden bulbs where its diminutive scale will not be lost, repotting and dividing offsets only when thoroughly dormant.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just below soil level in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun in fall; this Patagonian steppe species is among the most cold-tolerant Rhodophiala and wants a dry summer dormancy followed by cool, moist autumn and winter growth.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just below the soil surface in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun in fall, matching the dry grassland and steppe habitat of southern Chile and Argentina where it grows. Rhodophiala araucana sends up strap-like leaves in autumn or winter followed by a short stem bearing a small cluster of orange-red, amaryllis-like trumpet flowers in late spring to early summer, smaller and daintier than the related, more commonly grown Rhodophiala bifida. It is one of the hardiest Rhodophiala species thanks to its Patagonian origin and tolerates being left undisturbed and dry through summer dormancy far better than most South American bulbs. Grow it in a raised bed, rock garden, or container where summer rainfall can be controlled, and avoid any supplemental water once the foliage yellows.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers about 3 inches deep in fall into free-draining, humus-rich loam over chalk or limestone, in open woodland edges or unimproved calcareous grassland with dappled light.

directions: Military orchid produces a dense spike of pale lilac-pink, helmet-shaped flowers whose patterned lip, marked with darker spots and divided into slender limbs, resembles a tiny uniformed soldier, opening in late spring on open, unimproved calcareous grassland and sunny woodland margins across much of Europe. It needs more light than deep-shade woodland orchids but still benefits from humus-rich, chalk- or limestone-based soil that stays evenly moist without becoming waterlogged. As with other hardy terrestrial orchids, its tubers depend on an intact mycorrhizal fungal partner, so source only nursery-propagated stock from a specialist hardy orchid grower rather than attempting division or wild collection. Leave established plants undisturbed, avoid any fertilizer or fungicide near the root zone, and expect a very slow bulking-up over several years before a planting becomes showy.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall where winters are mild, or in very early spring as soon as soil can be worked; this large-flowered Turkish strain resents transplanting and should be seeded where it is to bloom, thinned rather than moved.

directions: Scatter seed thinly over prepared ground in fall or early spring and press in without deep covering, since this heirloom strain named for the Milas district of Turkey dislikes root disturbance as much as the common wild corncockle. It grows taller and carries noticeably larger, flatter, more rounded magenta-pink blooms than the typical species, each petal faintly veined and marked near the center, held on the same wiry, silver-hairy stems above narrow gray-green leaves. Grow it in lean to average soil in full sun among other cottage-garden annuals or at the back of a cutting bed, where the long stems make it useful in mixed bouquets. As with all corncockle, keep seed and plant material away from children, pets, and livestock, since it remains toxic if ingested.
